title: Shrewsbury Blues, first Imperial record
summary: Ridgley recounts singing near Shrewsbury Road, being signed through Dave Bartholomew and Al Young, and recording Shrewsbury Blues, his first release, and where Shrewsbury is.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, I wrote Shrewsbury Blues and I wrote the flip side, I think it was Early Dawn Boogie. And I tell you what, back then I was influenced by Roy Brown, T-Bone Walker, and mostly Roy Brown, because Roy Brown was very, very popular at that time. And I remember, see this is the beginning, this is right in the early stages of my singing career. I was singing on Shrewsbury Road by Sam Gennaro's place, and Bama had a Dixieland band there. And I used to go in there and sing, you know, and we would get a quarter, somebody would give us a quarter
and stuff for singing a specific song.

And I used to do Long About Midnight, but it was because I could sing ballads that really kind of take the musicians off. You know, I liked the idea, you know, I'd come in and sing, but I could sing ballads. Right. And so this was, you know, that was the very beginning. But Shrewsbury Blues, when I left Bama, and I went with Earl Anderson up in Gertown by the, what was it called?

Starlight. Yeah, okay. And I was singing, but that's when Dave Bitholomew, and I guess they heard about me, because Dave Bitholomew, Al Young, who had the record shop, one-stop record shop on Rampart Street, they came to listen to me. And I guess they liked what I heard, what they heard, because that Monday I had an appointment, and I met Dave Bitholomew, and at One Stop Record Shop with me, Al Young, and we went to Charles Levy's office, wherever that was, or somewhere. And, well, they signed me up. And I signed everything they put before me. And then I recorded Shrewsbury Blues, Early Dawn Boogie, and I guess I did Four Sides.
But I know, I know early enough Shrewsbury Blues was the first release.
And that was about Shrewsbury Blues?
Yeah, that was right down the causeway. It was Shrewsbury's location from...

Yeah, it's from, I say, from the river to the track, the first track. Because across the track... Which track? Well, it's Public Belt Railroad. Okay. See, that's right, that's right. That's that section, that's Shrewsbury. Now, and it's, I guess it's from La Bar Road all the way to Severn Avenue. Okay. Over, you know, in Whip. That's Shrewsbury.
Well, you're kind of right on the edge almost.
Yeah, I live, I live right on the, I was living on the causeway. Yeah. See, we used to call it Harlem Avenue.
Yeah, right. And, because that's where, that's where I grew up. Well, okay, I recorded Shrewsbury Blues and it was a big hit in Shrewsbury.
Yeah. Was it a big hit in New Orleans?

Yeah, well, it was a big hit in New Orleans. In fact, I have requests for it now. I don't remember that song. But it's in this album. Uh-huh, yeah. And, you know, I listened to, I listened to the record and, and it sound better now than it did then because I think they were able to take some hiss out and you get a little bit better quality of what you can hear now than a long time ago. But I used to hate that, you know, after, later on I listened to that bad sound. See, because in recording, Cosmo would look up and get a good sound. Good sound didn't come every day. You record me, maybe two, three, four, five different people come in and record. He didn't get no good sound and then he'd look up on one. But Shrewsbury Blues was my first release on Imperium.
